title: "PKI"
subtitle: "Inspect a certificate, explain issuance, and name the validation check that fails."
---

## Public key infrastructure

- **Public keys and private keys.** A key pair is two related keys. What one does, only the other can undo: data encrypted to the public key needs the private key to decrypt, and a signature made with the private key verifies with the public key. The private key never needs to leave its owner.
- **What a certificate does and does not prove.** A certificate is a signed statement from a certificate authority (CA): *this public key belongs to this name, for these uses, during this time*. It does not prove the site is safe, that the operator is who you assume, or that the private key has not been stolen since.
- **Certificate authorities and trust.** You trust a CA because a trust store says to: the operating system's, the browser's, or one you configured. A certificate is only as trustworthy as the CA that signed it and the store that trusts that CA.

The profile for certificates on the internet is [RFC 5280](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280.html).

## Sample files {#sample-files}

Training certificate and CSR samples. **Do not install the training root.** No private keys are included. The private training CA's lifetime is not a statement of public Web PKI issuance policy.

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [training-root.pem](files/samples/pki/training-root.pem) | Self-signed root CA, `CN=Squeaky Curd Root CA`, of the Cheese Curd Authority, PEM |
| [training-leaf.pem](files/samples/pki/training-leaf.pem) | Server certificate for `squeakycurds.example`, the Squeaky Curds Co-op of Curdsville, Wisconsin, issued by the root, PEM |
| [training-leaf.der](files/samples/pki/training-leaf.der) | The same leaf certificate, DER |
| [training-request.csr](files/samples/pki/training-request.csr) | The PKCS #10 request the leaf was issued from |

The chain is two levels: the root signs the leaf directly. Public CAs issue from an intermediate, as in the diagram below.

::: {.light-content}
![Root CA signs an intermediate, which signs the leaf. The client supplies the trust anchor; the server presents the leaf and intermediates.](files/images/certificate-chain.png){fig-alt="Certificate chain diagram: root CA, intermediate CA, leaf certificate."}
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![Root CA signs an intermediate, which signs the leaf. The client supplies the trust anchor; the server presents the leaf and intermediates.](files/images/certificate-chain-dark.png){fig-alt="Certificate chain diagram: root CA, intermediate CA, leaf certificate."}
:::

## What's in a certificate?

Output of `openssl x509 -in training-leaf.pem -noout -text`, modulus and signature trimmed:

```text
Certificate:
    Data:
        Version: 3 (0x2)
        Serial Number:
            55:25:8b:df:e8:83:4d:47:5c:a1:59:29:20:9e:59:cb:4f:92:68:17
        Signature Algorithm: sha256WithRSAEncryption
        Issuer: C=US, ST=Wisconsin, O=Cheese Curd Authority, CN=Squeaky Curd Root CA
        Validity
            Not Before: Oct  1 00:00:00 2026 GMT
            Not After : Oct  1 00:00:00 2027 GMT
        Subject: C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
        Subject Public Key Info:
            Public Key Algorithm: rsaEncryption
                Public-Key: (2048 bit)
                Modulus: 00:e5:37:5c:d1:85:f9:43:92: ...
                Exponent: 65537 (0x10001)
        X509v3 extensions:
            X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical
                CA:FALSE
            X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
                DNS:squeakycurds.example
            X509v3 Extended Key Usage:
                TLS Web Server Authentication
    Signature Algorithm: sha256WithRSAEncryption
    Signature Value: 49:06:a2:1b:9b:5a:6a:a3: ...
```

The root has `Basic Constraints: critical, CA:TRUE, pathlen:0` and `Key Usage: critical, Certificate Sign, CRL Sign`: it may sign certificates and CRLs, but no CA below it may.

### Field reference

| Field | What it holds | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Version | 3 for anything with extensions | Shown as `3 (0x2)`; the encoded value is zero-based |
| Serial number | Unique per issuing CA | Used to identify the certificate in CRLs and OCSP |
| Signature algorithm | How the CA signed it | `sha256WithRSAEncryption`, `ecdsa-with-SHA256` |
| Issuer | The CA's distinguished name | Must match the subject of the issuing certificate |
| Validity | Not Before, Not After | Always UTC in the certificate; tools may display local time |
| Subject | Distinguished name of the holder | For TLS, the name check uses the SAN, not the CN |
| Subject public key info | The public key and its algorithm | The private key is never in the certificate |
| Extensions | Everything else (below) | A **critical** extension a client does not understand must cause rejection |

**Distinguished names.** A DN is a sequence of attributes such as `CN` (common name, 2.5.4.3), `O` (organization, 2.5.4.10), `OU`, `L`, `ST` and `C`. [RFC 9525](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9525.html) §2 is explicit that "The Common Name RDN MUST NOT be used to identify a service"; clients match the requested name against the subject alternative name.

### Extensions and OIDs

| Extension | OID | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subject Alternative Name | 2.5.29.17 | The names the certificate is valid for: `DNS:`, `IP:`, `email:`, `URI:` |
| Basic Constraints | 2.5.29.19 | `CA:TRUE` or `CA:FALSE`, and an optional path length limit |
| Key Usage | 2.5.29.15 | Low-level operations: digitalSignature, keyEncipherment, keyCertSign, cRLSign |
| Extended Key Usage | 2.5.29.37 | Purposes: the OIDs below |
| Subject Key Identifier | 2.5.29.14 | Hash identifying this certificate's key |
| Authority Key Identifier | 2.5.29.35 | Identifies the issuer's key; helps chain building |
| CRL Distribution Points | 2.5.29.31 | Where to download the issuer's CRL |
| Authority Information Access | 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1.1 | Where to fetch the issuer certificate (caIssuers) and OCSP responder |
| Certificate Policies | 2.5.29.32 | Policy OIDs the CA issued under |

| Extended key usage | OID |
| --- | --- |
| TLS server authentication | 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1 |
| TLS client authentication | 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2 |
| Code signing | 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.3 |
| Email protection (S/MIME) | 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.4 |
| Time stamping | 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.8 |
| OCSP signing | 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.9 |
| Smart card logon (Microsoft) | 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.2 |

## Inspecting certificates

### certutil (Windows)

`certutil -dump` reads PEM or DER without being told which:

```powershell
certutil -dump training-leaf.pem
certutil -dump training-leaf.der
```

```text
X509 Certificate:
Version: 3
Serial Number: 55258bdfe8834d475ca15929209e59cb4f926817
Signature Algorithm:
    Algorithm ObjectId: 1.2.840.113549.1.1.11 sha256RSA
Issuer:
    CN=Squeaky Curd Root CA
    O=Cheese Curd Authority
    S=Wisconsin
    C=US

 NotBefore: 9/30/2026 7:00 PM
 NotAfter: 9/30/2027 7:00 PM

Subject:
    CN=squeakycurds.example
    O=Squeaky Curds Co-op
    L=Curdsville
    S=Wisconsin
    C=US
...
Cert Hash(sha256): 566d45250ce6aa7ff4c7db5576b81eb8b657c2c6067d5faa812d395bee69ae67
```

::: {.output-note}
certutil shows validity in local time (here US Central, UTC−5): `9/30/2026 7:00 PM` is `Oct 1 00:00:00 2026 GMT`. It also lists distinguished names in the opposite order from OpenSSL, and calls the state `S` rather than `ST`. When you compare timestamps across tools, check the time zone.
:::

### PowerShell and .NET

.NET reads certificate files directly. This function returns the fields you usually want, including the names in the SAN:

```powershell
{{< include ../scripts/Get-CertificateInfo.ps1 >}}
```

```powershell
Get-CertificateInfo -Path .\training-leaf.pem
```

```text
Subject      : CN=squeakycurds.example, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, L=Curdsville, S=Wisconsin, C=US
Issuer       : CN=Squeaky Curd Root CA, O=Cheese Curd Authority, S=Wisconsin, C=US
NotBefore    : 9/30/2026 7:00:00 PM
NotAfter     : 9/30/2027 7:00:00 PM
DnsNames     : squeakycurds.example
Thumbprint   : D3A4DAB5033F7341F308383338E64AF8C1CD56C3
SerialNumber : 55258BDFE8834D475CA15929209E59CB4F926817
```

To see every extension with its OID:

```powershell
$Cert = [System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates.X509Certificate2]::new((Resolve-Path .\training-leaf.pem).Path)
$Cert.Extensions | ForEach-Object { '{0} ({1}): {2}' -f $_.Oid.FriendlyName, $_.Oid.Value, $_.Format($false) }
```

```text
Basic Constraints (2.5.29.19): Subject Type=End Entity, Path Length Constraint=None
Subject Alternative Name (2.5.29.17): DNS Name=squeakycurds.example
Enhanced Key Usage (2.5.29.37): Server Authentication (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1)
```

The Windows **thumbprint** is the SHA-1 hash of the DER certificate. It identifies a certificate in a store; it is not a security property.

Certificates already installed on a machine are in the `Cert:` drive:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My |
	Select-Object Subject, NotAfter, Thumbprint,
		@{ n = 'San'; e = { ($_.Extensions | Where-Object { $_.Oid.Value -eq '2.5.29.17' }).Format($false) } }

Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My -ExpiringInDays 30
```

### OpenSSL

```bash
openssl x509 -in training-leaf.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
openssl x509 -in training-leaf.pem -noout -fingerprint -sha256
openssl x509 -in training-leaf.der -inform der -noout -fingerprint -sha256
openssl asn1parse -in training-leaf.pem        # the raw ASN.1 structure
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts </dev/null   # what a live server presents
```

#### Installing OpenSSL on Windows

The OpenSSL project publishes source code only; Windows builds come from third parties, listed on the project's [binaries page](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/wiki/Binaries). Any of these works:

| Option | How | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Git for Windows | Already installed with Git | `C:\Program Files\Git\mingw64\bin\openssl.exe`; on the `PATH` in Git Bash, not in PowerShell |
| Shining Light Productions | `winget install ShiningLight.OpenSSL.Light` | Long-standing Win64 installer; `ShiningLight.OpenSSL.LTS.Light` tracks the long-term-support 3.5 branch |
| FireDaemon | `winget install FireDaemon.OpenSSL` | Signed builds, also offered as a zip for portable use |
| Chocolatey | `choco install openssl` | |
| Scoop | `scoop install openssl` | Per-user, no administrator rights needed |

After installing, open a new PowerShell window and run `openssl version`. If an older copy answers instead, `Get-Command openssl -All` lists every copy on the `PATH`, in the order they are found.

### XCA

[XCA](https://hohnstaedt.de/xca/) is my preferred graphical tool for certificates. It opens certificates, requests, keys, CRLs and PKCS #12 files, shows every field and extension, and can run a small CA with templates for test work. Keys are stored in an encrypted database. Install it from the [XCA site](https://hohnstaedt.de/xca/), the Microsoft Store, `winget install ChristianHohnstadt.xca` or `choco install xca`. Import `training-root.pem` and `training-leaf.pem` to see the chain.

## Certificate formats

- **ASN.1** describes the structure. **DER** is the binary encoding of that structure.
- **PEM** is Base64 DER between `-----BEGIN ...-----` and `-----END ...-----` lines ([RFC 7468](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7468.html)). The label says what is inside: `CERTIFICATE`, `CERTIFICATE REQUEST`, `PRIVATE KEY`, `PKCS7`.
- A file extension does not necessarily tell you what's inside.

| Extension | Usually holds | Contains a private key? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.cer`, `.crt` | One certificate, DER or PEM | No |
| `.pem` | Anything PEM: certificates, chains, keys, CSRs | Possibly; look at the labels |
| `.key` | A private key, usually PEM | Yes |
| `.p7b`, `.p7c` | PKCS #7 / CMS bundle of certificates ([RFC 5652](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5652.html)) | No |
| `.pfx`, `.p12` | PKCS #12 archive: certificate, chain and private key, password protected ([RFC 7292](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7292.html)) | Usually yes |
| `.csr`, `.req` | PKCS #10 certificate request | No |

**Same certificate, two encodings.** `training-leaf.pem` and `training-leaf.der` are the same certificate. Their certificate fingerprints match:

```text
sha256 Fingerprint=56:6D:45:25:0C:E6:AA:7F:F4:C7:DB:55:76:B8:1E:B8:B6:57:C2:C6:06:7D:5F:AA:81:2D:39:5B:EE:69:AE:67
```

The SHA-256 **file** hash of the DER file is the same value, because a certificate fingerprint is the hash of its DER encoding. The PEM file's hash differs, because it is text.

### Converting

```bash
openssl x509 -in training-leaf.der -inform der -out leaf.pem          # DER to PEM
openssl x509 -in training-leaf.pem -outform der -out leaf.der         # PEM to DER
openssl pkcs7 -in bundle.p7b -print_certs -out bundle.pem             # PKCS #7 to PEM certificates
openssl pkcs12 -in server.pfx -nokeys -out server-certs.pem           # certificates out of a PFX
```

```powershell
certutil -encode training-leaf.der leaf.pem     # DER to PEM (Base64)
certutil -decode training-leaf.pem leaf.der     # PEM to DER
```

## Certificate requests and issuance

### Certificate signing requests (PKCS #10)

A CSR ([RFC 2986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2986.html)) carries the public key, the requested subject and requested extensions, signed with the matching private key. The signature proves the requester holds the private key; it proves nothing about whether they should get the name. That is the CA's job.

```bash
openssl req -in training-request.csr -noout -text -verify
```

```text
Certificate request self-signature verify OK
Certificate Request:
    Data:
        Version: 1 (0x0)
        Subject: C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
        ...
        Attributes:
            Requested Extensions:
                X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
                    DNS:squeakycurds.example
```

The CSR and the issued certificate carry the same public key:

```bash
openssl req  -in training-request.csr -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
openssl x509 -in training-leaf.pem    -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
# both: 7a764e059181f774138b29119eab1ab71dce68e5829aba787c3a7f3fb9deecb0
```

Creating a key pair and request with OpenSSL (the key stays with you):

```bash
openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout server.key -out server.csr \
	-subj "/CN=squeakycurds.example" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:squeakycurds.example"
```

### Internal CAs: AD CS and certificate templates

Active Directory Certificate Services issues against **certificate templates**, which set key usage, EKU, validity, who may enroll and whether the subject comes from the request or from AD. Request with [`certreq`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/certreq_1) and an INF file:

```ini
[NewRequest]
Subject = "CN=squeakycurds.example"
KeyAlgorithm = RSA
KeyLength = 2048
Exportable = FALSE
MachineKeySet = TRUE
RequestType = PKCS10

[Extensions]
2.5.29.17 = "{text}"
_continue_ = "dns=squeakycurds.example&"

[RequestAttributes]
CertificateTemplate = WebServer
```

```powershell
certreq -new request.inf request.csr        # create the key pair and request
certreq -submit -config "CA01\Contoso Issuing CA" request.csr server.cer
certreq -accept server.cer                  # install, pairing with the pending private key
```

Replace `CA01\Contoso Issuing CA` with your `CAHost\CA name`. The `CertificateTemplate` line needs a domain-joined machine that can see the template; without one, `certreq -new` reports "Template not found." To make a request without AD CS, remove that line and set `MachineKeySet = FALSE`.

Template settings that let the requester supply the subject name, combined with a client authentication EKU and broad enrollment rights, are a well-known AD CS privilege escalation path ("ESC1" in SpecterOps' [Certified Pre-Owned](https://specterops.io/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2022/06/Certified_Pre-Owned.pdf)). Review who can enroll in such templates.

### ACME and automated issuance

ACME ([RFC 8555](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8555.html)) automates the whole cycle: create an account, place an order for names, prove control of each name, send a CSR, download the certificate, renew before expiry. Proof of control is a **challenge**:

| Challenge | How control is proven | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `http-01` | Serve a token at `http://<name>/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>` on port 80 | No wildcards |
| `dns-01` | Publish a TXT record at `_acme-challenge.<name>` | Works for wildcards and internal-only hosts with public DNS |
| `tls-alpn-01` | Present a special certificate on port 443 ([RFC 8737](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8737.html)) | No wildcards |

The CA checks control of the name, then issues; it does not check who you are. That is domain validation.

## Putting a certificate to use

A service needs three things:

1. **The certificate.**
2. **The private key** that matches it.
3. **The intermediate certificates** between it and a root clients trust.

The certificate presented by a service is separate from the trust configured on a client. The server sends its leaf and intermediates; the client supplies the root from its own store. A server that omits its intermediate can work in one browser, which has the intermediate cached or fetches it from the AIA URL, and fail in another client, such as a script, an appliance or a mail server, that does neither.

On Windows the private key lives with the certificate in the store (or in a `.pfx`). On Linux it is usually a separate PEM file. Check that a certificate and key match by comparing public keys:

```bash
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
openssl pkey -in server.key -pubout | openssl sha256
```

## Certificate validation

[RFC 5280](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280.html) §6 defines path validation; [RFC 9525](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9525.html) defines name matching for TLS. A client checks:

| Check | Question | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name | Does a SAN entry match the name I asked for? | Wrong host, missing SAN, CN-only certificate |
| Dates | Is now between Not Before and Not After, for every certificate in the chain? | Expired, not yet valid, wrong clock |
| Chain | Can I build a path to a certificate in my trust store, with valid signatures? | Missing intermediate, untrusted or private root |
| Constraints | Is every issuer a CA, within its path length? | `CA:FALSE` certificate used as an issuer |
| Usage | Do key usage and EKU permit this purpose? | Server certificate used for client authentication |
| Revocation | Has the CA revoked anything in the chain? | Revoked; or, depending on client, status unavailable |

### Validation failures, reproduced

Each of these was run against the sample files with OpenSSL 3.5.

**Untrusted root** (the root is not in any trust store):

```text
$ openssl verify training-leaf.pem
C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
error 20 at 0 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer certificate
error training-leaf.pem: verification failed
```

Supplying the root as a trust anchor makes it pass: `openssl verify -CAfile training-root.pem training-leaf.pem` returns `training-leaf.pem: OK`.

**Incorrect name:**

```text
$ openssl verify -CAfile training-root.pem -verify_hostname www.squeakycurds.example training-leaf.pem
C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
error 62 at 0 depth lookup: hostname mismatch
error training-leaf.pem: verification failed
```

`squeakycurds.example` passes; `www.squeakycurds.example` does not, because the SAN lists only `squeakycurds.example`. A wildcard `*.squeakycurds.example` would match `www.squeakycurds.example` but not `squeakycurds.example` or `a.b.squeakycurds.example` (RFC 9525 §6.3).

**Expired** (checking as of December 1, 2027):

```text
$ openssl verify -CAfile training-root.pem -attime 1827619200 training-leaf.pem
C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
error 10 at 0 depth lookup: certificate has expired
error training-leaf.pem: verification failed
```

Checking as of September 1, 2026 reports `error 9 at 1 depth lookup: certificate is not yet valid`: depth 1 is the root, which was not yet valid either.

**Wrong usage** (the leaf's EKU is server authentication only):

```text
$ openssl verify -CAfile training-root.pem -purpose sslclient training-leaf.pem
C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
error 26 at 0 depth lookup: unsuitable certificate purpose
error training-leaf.pem: verification failed
```

**Windows view of the untrusted root.** `certutil -verify training-leaf.pem` on a machine without the training root:

```text
A certificate chain could not be built to a trusted root authority. 0x800b010a (-2146762486 CERT_E_CHAINING)
------------------------------------
Incomplete certificate chain
Cannot find certificate:
    CN=Squeaky Curd Root CA, O=Cheese Curd Authority, S=Wisconsin, C=US
Cert is an End Entity certificate

ERROR: Verifying leaf certificate revocation status returned The revocation function was unable to check revocation because the revocation server was offline. 0x80092013 (-2146885613 CRYPT_E_REVOCATION_OFFLINE)
CertUtil: The revocation function was unable to check revocation because the revocation server was offline.

CertUtil: -verify command completed successfully.
```

Note the last line: certutil reports the *command* completed, not that the certificate is valid. Read the errors above it. `certutil -verify -urlfetch` also retrieves AIA and CRL URLs and reports each one, which is the quickest way to find a broken CRL distribution point on an internal CA.

### Revocation: CRLs and OCSP

- **CRL** (Certificate Revocation List): a signed list of revoked serial numbers the CA publishes at the URL in the CRL Distribution Points extension. Clients download and cache it.
- **OCSP** (Online Certificate Status Protocol): ask the CA's responder about one certificate. Responses can be **stapled** by the server so the client does not have to ask.

Client behavior varies, and is the part people get wrong:

- **Browsers mostly do not check online.** Chrome relies on [CRLSets](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/crlsets/), a curated list pushed with updates, rather than fetching CRLs or OCSP for most certificates. Other browsers have their own approaches, so test the client you care about.
- **Public CAs are moving away from OCSP.** Let's Encrypt ended its OCSP service on August 6, 2025 and now publishes revocation only through CRLs ([announcement](https://letsencrypt.org/2025/08/06/ocsp-service-has-reached-end-of-life)).
- **Windows** (CryptoAPI) checks CRLs and OCSP and caches results. Whether "revocation server offline" is fatal depends on the application: some fail closed, many fail open.
- **Internal CAs** most often break here: an expired CRL or an unreachable CDP URL causes failures in clients that do enforce revocation, such as smart card logon on domain controllers and some VPNs.

## Renewal and maintenance

Expiration is the most common certificate incident, and public certificate lifetimes are getting shorter. The CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements (§1.2.2, from ballot SC-081v3, passed April 2025) set the maximum validity of publicly trusted TLS certificates:

| Issued on or after | Maximum validity |
| --- | ---: |
| March 15, 2026 | 200 days |
| March 15, 2027 | 100 days |
| March 15, 2029 | 47 days |

Source: [CA/Browser Forum TLS Baseline Requirements](https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/baseline-requirements/requirements/). These limits do not apply to private internal CAs, which set their own policy.

What renewal involves, and what tends to be missed:

- **An inventory.** Know which certificates exist, where they are deployed, and when they expire. For Windows, `Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My -ExpiringInDays 30` on each server; for anything listening on TLS, scan it.
- **Replacing, not just renewing.** A renewed certificate must be installed and bound everywhere the old one was: load balancers, IIS bindings, RDP, LDAPS, appliances, and anything that pinned the old one.
- **The new chain.** A renewal can come from a different intermediate. Deploy the chain the CA gives you with the new certificate.
- **Automation.** At 47 days, renewing by hand stops being realistic. ACME clients, AD CS autoenrollment and vendor integrations do the work; monitoring confirms it happened.
